newsitem.title: LEBANON: Beirut's Allied Business Bank plans mutual fund.
newsitem.headline: Beirut's Allied Business Bank plans mutual fund.

text.p: Beirut's Allied Business Bank (ABB) announced on Monday the launch of a financial company that will create mutual funds enabling small investors to invest in Lebanese paper.

ABB said in a statement that Allied Business Investment Corporation (ABICORP), whose establishment was approved by the central bank in September, will first launch a $1 million mutual fund "Golden Basket" to test the market.

"For the first time in the Lebanese financial market, ABICORP will provide a unique chance for all Lebanese to invest in the market for Lebanese shares and bills...by subscription in a basket of shares and bonds which ABICORP intends to launch after getting the Bank of Lebanon's approval," the bank said.
The fund will be the first in Lebanon based solely on Lebanese equities and bills.

Beirut investment house Capital Investment Services and the Royal Bank of Canada launched more than a year ago a fund called the International Lebanese Investment Account based on overseas and domestic equities and fixed-interest debt instruments.
Allied Business Bank, which ranked 30th among Beirut's 82 commercial banks in size of deposits in 1994, has a large stake in ABICORP but there are other shareholders in the venture, it said.

ABB General Manager Habib Abu Fadel told a news conference the open-ended mutual fund would initially sell to small investors shares derived from the stocks of the five companies currently listed on the Beirut Stock Exchange.
Other funds could be set up later to sell fund shares based on the shares of other listed or unlisted companies, he added.
"We thought these five shares should be the Golden Basket's nucleus," he said, adding that establishment of the fund was awaiting the approval of the Bank of Lebanon.
"This fund is one of ABICORP's investment funds which have precise and registered goals in Beirut, and which follow Lebanese trade law and the financial companies' law," the bank said.

Purchase of the fund's shares could be made in instalments, it added. To ensure a wide base of participants, the maximum available for each investor has been set at $10,000 -- or 100 shares -- and the minimum investment would be $500 for five shares.
"This gives the Lebanese investor of medium finances the chance to enter the Beirut bourse and have Lebanese shares," Abu Fadel said.
He said the fund would boost trade on the Beirut Stock Exchange, which has been lacklustre since it re-opened in January 1995 after a 13-year closure.
The only shares that change hands on a daily basis are those of Lebanon's largest company Solidere. The four other listed companies are Ciments Libanais, Ciments Blancs, Eternit and Uniceramic.
He said ABICORP also wanted to reach the large Lebanese diaspora and would advertise the fund in the Gulf and Europe.
